options: An object that orbits another object in space
Any device that transmits radio signals
A tool used only for weather forecasting
A type of aircraft that flies above 40,000 feet
explain: A satellite is an object that orbits another object in space, held in orbit by the gravitational pull of the larger object and the speed at which it travels.

q: What keeps a satellite in a consistent orbit?
options: Solar panels and battery power
The gravitational pull of the larger object and the satellite's speed
Radio signals from ground stations
Magnetic fields generated by the satellite
explain: Satellites are held in a consistent orbit by the gravitational pull of the larger object they circulate and the speed at which they travel.

q: Which of these is an example of a naturally occurring satellite?
options: Landsat 9
The International Space Station
The Moon
A GPS satellite
explain: The Moon is an example of a naturally occurring satellite that orbits Earth, while Landsat 9 is human-made.

q: Why are weather satellites described as geostationary?
options: They orbit the Earth at the same rotation speed as Earth, staying fixed over the same spot
They never move once launched into space
They only operate during daylight hours
They orbit only over the equator at high speed
explain: Weather satellites are geostationary, meaning they orbit the Earth at the same rotation speed as Earth, thereby staying fixed over the same spot on Earth.

q: How do GPS-enabled devices calculate position, speed, and altitude?
options: By measuring the brightness of the satellite signal
Based on the time delay between the GPS receiver and the satellite
By counting the number of visible satellites
Through a direct radio conversation with a ground station
explain: GPS-enabled devices pick up signals from orbiting satellites and calculate position, speed, and altitude based on the time delay between the GPS receiver and the satellite.

q: How does satellite imagery help farmers with crop management?
options: By physically spraying pesticides on crops
By capturing wavelengths reflected by plants to calculate spectral indices as proxy measurements of plant health
By replacing the need for any ground-based field data
By controlling irrigation systems directly
explain: Vegetation reflects light differently depending on plant health. Satellite imagery captures these reflected wavelengths and calculates spectral indices, which provide proxy measurements of plant health, helping farmers with crop management at scale.

q: What is a key advantage satellites have over drones and planes?
options: Lower launch cost
Global coverage and regular revisit times
Higher spatial resolution than drones
No dependency on weather conditions
explain: Satellites offer global coverage, regular revisit times, high operational lifespan, low data cost, consistent data quality, and historical data availability.

q: What distinguishes a satellite in low Earth orbit that is in sun-synchronous orbit?
options: It only orbits during the day
It passes over the equator at the same local time each day
It stays fixed over one point on Earth
It orbits only near the equator
explain: A satellite is in sun-synchronous orbit when the timing of it passing over the equator occurs at the same time each day.

q: What type of orbit do GPS satellites typically use?
options: Geostationary orbit
Molniya orbit
Semi-synchronous orbit
Sun-synchronous polar orbit
explain: GPS satellites use a semi-synchronous orbit, rotating in a near-polar orbit at a speed that allows them to pass the equator at the same spot twice each day.

q: What is unique about a satellite in a Molniya orbit?
options: It moves at a constant speed throughout its orbit
Its orbit is off-centered from Earth, so its speed changes depending on proximity to Earth
It only orbits above the equator
It is used exclusively for GPS navigation
explain: A Molniya orbit is off-centered from the Earth, causing the satellite to move at a higher speed when closer to Earth and slower when at the far side of its oval orbit. This pattern is used for communication near the poles.

options: A single large satellite with many complex instruments
A group of small satellites working together to collect data or transmit information
A satellite that has stopped functioning
A cluster of stars visible from a satellite's camera
explain: Small satellites working together are referred to as artificial satellite constellations, which can consist of a few to thousands of satellites and allow a short revisit time between passes over a location.

q: What term describes a sensor positioned directly over its object of interest at a 0° viewing angle?
options: Off-nadir
Look angle
Nadir
Zenith
explain: Satellites positioned directly over the object of interest have their sensors positioned at nadir, or a 0° viewing angle.

q: What trade-off comes with positioning a sensor at an angle away from nadir?
options: Images become completely unusable
Images capture the sides of objects and cover larger areas, with increased temporal resolution, but reduced clarity
Only the color of the image changes
The satellite must slow down its orbit
explain: Sensors positioned nadir result in images with high clarity, while sensors positioned at an angle away from nadir capture the sides of objects of interest, cover larger areas, and increase temporal resolution.

q: Which term describes a satellite's rotation around its forward-flight axis?
options: Yaw
Pitch
Roll
Azimuth
explain: Roll defines the rotation of the satellite around its forward-flight axis.
